items.stem: A robot arm must grasp parts whose exact 3D position varies. Which vision capability most directly provides what the gripper needs?

options.text: Pose estimation that recovers the object's position and orientation
options.rationale: Correct: grasping needs the object's 6-DoF pose, which pose estimation provides.

options.text: A colour histogram of the whole image
options.rationale: A global colour histogram does not locate or orient the object.
Resolution alone does not yield the object's pose.
Grayscale conversion does not estimate position or orientation.

items.explanation: Correct: grasping needs the object's 6-DoF pose, which pose estimation provides.

items.stem: Which TWO are valid ways for a robot to perceive depth? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Stereo vision using the disparity between two cameras
A time-of-flight or structured-light depth sensor
options.rationale: Correct: active depth sensors measure distance directly.

options.text: A single uncalibrated 2D photo read as exact metric distances
options.rationale: One ordinary 2D image does not give metric depth without extra cues.

options.text: Counting the number of pixels in the image
options.rationale: Pixel count is resolution, not depth.

items.stem: Why is camera calibration important in a vision-guided robot?

options.text: It relates image pixels to real-world geometry so measurements and poses are accurate
options.rationale: Correct: calibration maps pixels to metric space, enabling accurate positioning.

options.text: It makes the camera capture images faster
options.rationale: Calibration concerns geometry, not frame rate.

options.text: It removes the need for any lighting
options.rationale: Calibration does not address scene lighting.

options.text: It encrypts the image for security
options.rationale: Calibration is geometric, not a security measure.

items.explanation: Correct: calibration maps pixels to metric space, enabling accurate positioning.
